claim: Ants use debris as tools to collect and transport liquid food to the nest.
source: Ants use debris as tools to collect and transport liquid food to the nest.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous work throughout the manuscript.

claim: Tool use in ants is flexible whereby ants learn to use artificial material that is novel to them and select tools with optimal soaking properties.
source: Previous studies showed that this behaviour is flexible whereby ants learn to use artificial material that is novel to them and select tools with optimal soaking properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to previous studies.

claim: Only a small number of workers performed tool use in Aphaenogaster senilis.
source: Only a small number of workers performed tool use and they did it repeatedly, although they also collected solid food.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Workers that performed tool use did it repeatedly.
source: Only a small number of workers performed tool use and they did it repeatedly, although they also collected solid food.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing repeated tool use within and across trials.

claim: Tool users also collected solid food.
source: Only a small number of workers performed tool use and they did it repeatedly, although they also collected solid food.
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 2 showing that about half of workers transporting cricket legs were also tool users.

claim: Personality predicted the probability to perform tool use in Aphaenogaster senilis.
source: Personality predicted the probability to perform tool use: ants that showed higher exploratory activity and were more attracted to a prey in the personality tests became the new tool users when previous tool users were removed from the group.
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 3, supported by statistical analysis showing personality score significantly predicted tool use probability.

claim: Ants that showed higher exploratory activity became tool users when previous tool users were removed.
source: Personality predicted the probability to perform tool use: ants that showed higher exploratory activity and were more attracted to a prey in the personality tests became the new tool users when previous tool users were removed from the group.
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 3 showing correlation between personality traits and tool use behavior.

claim: Ants that were more attracted to prey became tool users when previous tool users were removed.
source: Personality predicted the probability to perform tool use: ants that showed higher exploratory activity and were more attracted to a prey in the personality tests became the new tool users when previous tool users were removed from the group.
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 3 showing correlation between reaction to prey and tool use behavior.

claim: Variation in personality traits within the colony may improve division of labour instead of extreme task specialisation.
source: This suggests that, instead of extreme task specialisation, variation in personality traits within the colony may improve division of labour.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings and theoretical considerations about division of labour.

claim: Tool use is defined as the external employment of an unattached or manipulable attached environmental object to alter more efficiently the form, position, or condition of another object, another organism, or the user itself, when the user holds and directly manipulates the tool during or prior to use and is responsible for the proper and effective orientation of the tool.
source: Tool use is defined as "the external employment of an unattached or manipulable attached environmental object to alter more efficiently the form, position, or condition of another object, another organism, or the user itself, when the user holds and directly manipulates the tool during or prior to use and is responsible for the proper and effective orientation of the tool" (Shumaker et al., 2011, p. 5).
evidence: This is a definition cited from Shumaker et al., 2011.

claim: Tool use in pigs was recently discovered.
source: Tool use is a widespread phenomenon within the animal kingdom (Shumaker et al., 2011; Sanz et al., 2013) and new examples of animal tool use are regularly discovered, such as recently in pigs (Root-Bernstein et al., 2019) and seabirds (Fayet et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Root-Bernstein et al., 2019.

claim: Tool use in seabirds was recently discovered.
source: Tool use is a widespread phenomenon within the animal kingdom (Shumaker et al., 2011; Sanz et al., 2013) and new examples of animal tool use are regularly discovered, such as recently in pigs (Root-Bernstein et al., 2019) and seabirds (Fayet et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fayet et al., 2020.

claim: Smith and Bentley-Condit, 2010 reported about 50 cases of tool use in insects, encompassing 30 different genera.
source: Smith and Bentley-Condit, 2010 reported about 50 cases of tool use in insects, encompassing 30 different genera.
evidence: This is a factual claim supported by citation to Smith and Bentley-Condit, 2010.

claim: Some species of ants use debris to transport liquid food.
source: Among the best described examples is the use of debris to transport liquid food by some species of ants (Morrill, 1972; Barber et al., 1989), in particular, several species of the genus Aphaenogaster (Fellers and Fellers, 1976; Tanaka and Ono, 1978; McDonald, 1984; Agbogba, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Workers of Aphaenogaster species are characterised by the lack of a distensible crop.
source: Workers of these species are characterised by the lack of a distensible crop and by a chitinous gaster, preventing the transportation of large amounts of liquid food inside their bodies, a feature common in many other ant species (Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990; Davidson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990 and Davidson et al., 2004.

claim: Workers of Aphaenogaster species have a chitinous gaster, preventing the transportation of large amounts of liquid food inside their bodies.
source: Workers of these species are characterised by the lack of a distensible crop and by a chitinous gaster, preventing the transportation of large amounts of liquid food inside their bodies, a feature common in many other ant species (Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990; Davidson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990 and Davidson et al., 2004.

claim: Aphaenogaster workers do not perform mouth-to-mouth exchange of liquid food (trophallaxis).
source: Moreover, unlike most ant species, Aphaenogaster workers do not perform mouth-to-mouth exchange of liquid food (i.e. trophallaxis, Delage and Jaisson, 1969); therefore, foragers cannot use this form of food transmission among colony members.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Delage and Jaisson, 1969.

claim: Aphaenogaster foragers cannot use trophallaxis for food transmission among colony members.
source: Moreover, unlike most ant species, Aphaenogaster workers do not perform mouth-to-mouth exchange of liquid food (i.e. trophallaxis, Delage and Jaisson, 1969); therefore, foragers cannot use this form of food transmission among colony members.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the fact that they do not perform trophallaxis.

claim: Aphaenogaster workers forage individually mostly on the ground level.
source: Workers forage individually mostly on the ground level and can cover large areas in habitats with scarce food sources (Cerdá et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cerdá et al., 1998.

claim: Aphaenogaster workers can cover large areas in habitats with scarce food sources.
source: Workers forage individually mostly on the ground level and can cover large areas in habitats with scarce food sources (Cerdá et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cerdá et al., 1998.

claim: When Aphaenogaster foragers discover liquid food, they collect debris, drop them into the liquid food, and then transport these soaked debris to their nest.
source: When Aphaenogaster foragers discover a source of liquid food, such as fruit pulp or body fluids of dead insects, they collect debris (pieces of leaves, soil, sand grains), drop them into the liquid food, and then transport these soaked debris to their nest.
evidence: This is a description of observed behavior supported by general knowledge of the species.

claim: The behavior of Aphaenogaster ants dropping debris into liquid food and transporting it qualifies as tool use, namely tool-assisted food transport.
source: This behaviour qualifies as tool use, namely tool-assisted food transport.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the definition of tool use and observed behavior.

claim: Aphaenogaster ants do not drop debris in non-food substances.
source: Indeed, these ants do not drop debris in non-food substances (Banschbach et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Banschbach et al., 2006.

claim: Aphaenogaster ant workers prefer materials that are easy to handle and with good soaking capacity.
source: In a previous study (Maák et al., 2017), we have investigated whether Aphaenogaster ants are selective in the choice of material to be used as tools and we demonstrated that ant workers prefer materials that are easy to handle and with good soaking capacity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maák et al., 2017.

claim: Aphaenogaster ants can learn to use artificial material that is novel to them.
source: Furthermore, ants can learn to use artificial material that is novel to them and select the material with optimal soaking properties, thus showing that tool use is not behaviourally fixed in ants (Maák et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maák et al., 2017.

claim: Tool use is not behaviourally fixed in ants.
source: Furthermore, ants can learn to use artificial material that is novel to them and select the material with optimal soaking properties, thus showing that tool use is not behaviourally fixed in ants (Maák et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation to Maák et al., 2017.

claim: Tool selection in Aphaenogaster depends on the foraging environment and varies with food type (viscosity), distance, and availability of tools.
source: Tool selection also depends on the foraging environment and varies with food type (viscosity), distance, and availability of tools (Lőrinczi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lőrinczi et al., 2018.

claim: In A. rudis, the tool use behaviour is carried out by a small subset of individuals within the group of foragers.
source: In A. rudis, it was observed that the tool use behaviour is carried out by a small subset of individuals within the group of foragers and only a small number of workers perform the debris dropping task (Banschbach et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Banschbach et al., 2006.

claim: In A. subterranea, the proportion of workers observed to use tools was only a small fraction of the total number of foragers.
source: In A. subterranea as well, the proportion of workers observed to use tools was only a small fraction of the total number of foragers.
evidence: This is supported by citation context referring to Lőrinczi, 2014.

claim: In A. subterranea, the number of tool users did not increase with colony size, while the number of total foragers did.
source: The number of tool users did not increase with colony size, while the number of total foragers did.
evidence: This is supported by citation context referring to Lőrinczi, 2014.

claim: In A. subterranea, there was no significant relationship between the number of ants working at the debris dropping task and the number of debris pieces dropped.
source: Moreover, there was no significant relationship between the number of ants working at the debris dropping task and the number of debris pieces dropped, indicating that a small number of workers can perform this task very efficiently (Lőrinczi, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lőrinczi, 2014.

claim: A small number of workers can perform the debris dropping task very efficiently in A. subterranea.
source: Moreover, there was no significant relationship between the number of ants working at the debris dropping task and the number of debris pieces dropped, indicating that a small number of workers can perform this task very efficiently (Lőrinczi, 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on data cited from Lőrinczi, 2014.

claim: When inter-individual differences in behavioural traits are consistent across time and/or context they are considered personality traits.
source: When inter-individual differences in behavioural traits are consistent across time and/or context they are considered personality traits (Réale and Dingemanse, 2012).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to Réale and Dingemanse, 2012.

claim: Both workers and colonies of ants can show personalities.
source: In ants, both workers and colonies can show personalities (Pinter-Wollman, 2012) and there is a link between individual and collective behaviour (Carere et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pinter-Wollman, 2012 and Carere et al., 2018.

claim: There is a link between individual and collective behaviour in ants.
source: In ants, both workers and colonies can show personalities (Pinter-Wollman, 2012) and there is a link between individual and collective behaviour (Carere et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carere et al., 2018.

claim: In the ant Leptothorax acervorum, more exploratory and aggressive workers were also more active in the nest (rested less).
source: There is some evidence that the allocation of workers to a certain task may be influenced by individual personality, for instance in the ant Leptothorax acervorum (Kühbandner et al., 2014), where more exploratory and aggressive workers were also more active in the nest (rested less).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kühbandner et al., 2014.

claim: Inter-individual difference in personality could enhance division of labour.
source: This inter-individual difference could enhance division of labour (Jeanson and Weidenmüller, 2014), the phenomenon in which different individuals perform different tasks.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citation to Jeanson and Weidenmüller, 2014.

claim: Division of labour is beneficial for colony organisation.
source: Division of labour is beneficial for colony organisation and it is believed to be one of the principal factors explaining the extraordinary ecological success of social insects (Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Division of labour is believed to be one of the principal factors explaining the extraordinary ecological success of social insects.
source: Division of labour is beneficial for colony organisation and it is believed to be one of the principal factors explaining the extraordinary ecological success of social insects (Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990 and represents established knowledge.

claim: The 'response threshold model' posits that individual workers differ in their sensory perception and/or in their behavioural responses to stimuli associated with specific tasks.
source: A broadly acknowledged model explaining the emergence of division of labour within a colony is the 'response threshold model', which posits that individual workers differ in their sensory perception and/or in their behavioural responses to stimuli associated with specific tasks (Robinson, 1992; Beshers and Fewell, 2001).
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical model supported by citations to Robinson, 1992 and Beshers and Fewell, 2001.

claim: There is an association between personality traits and cognitive traits in ants.
source: We also know that there is an association between personality traits and cognitive traits in ants.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent citations to studies on carpenter ants.

claim: Consistent individual differences in exploratory activity predicted learning performance of individual carpenter ants, with 'active-explorers' being slower in learning than 'inactive-explorers'.
source: Consistent individual differences in exploratory activity predicted learning performance of individual carpenter ants, with 'active-explorers' being slower in learning than 'inactive-explorers' (Udino et al., 2017) and individual differences in exploratory activity were linked to cognitive judgement bias, the propensity to anticipate either positive or negative consequences in response to ambiguous information (d'Ettorre et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Udino et al., 2017.

claim: Individual differences in exploratory activity in carpenter ants were linked to cognitive judgement bias.
source: Consistent individual differences in exploratory activity predicted learning performance of individual carpenter ants, with 'active-explorers' being slower in learning than 'inactive-explorers' (Udino et al., 2017) and individual differences in exploratory activity were linked to cognitive judgement bias, the propensity to anticipate either positive or negative consequences in response to ambiguous information (d'Ettorre et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to d'Ettorre et al., 2017.

claim: The number of workers present in the foraging arena before replacing the bridge had a positive effect on the latency to drop the first tools into the bait.
source: The results show that the number of workers present in the foraging arena before replacing the bridge had a positive effect on the latency to drop the first tools into the bait (LMM t = −2.22, N = 15, p=0.047), meaning that the higher the number of workers present, the shorter the latency.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: The higher the number of workers present in the foraging arena, the shorter the latency to drop the first tool into the bait.
source: The results show that the number of workers present in the foraging arena before replacing the bridge had a positive effect on the latency to drop the first tools into the bait (LMM t = −2.22, N = 15, p=0.047), meaning that the higher the number of workers present, the shorter the latency.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical result from Experiment 1.

claim: The shorter the latency to drop the first tool into the bait, the shorter the total time needed to transport all the tools to the bait.
source: Also, the shorter was the latency to drop the first tool into the bait, the shorter the total time needed to transport all the tools to the bait (t = 2.26, N = 15, p=0.043).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: The number of workers involved in tool use did not have any effect on the latency to drop the first tool to the bait.
source: However, the number of workers involved in tool use did not have any effect on the latency to drop the first tool to the bait (t = 1.34, N = 15, p=0.20) nor on the total time of tool transport to the bait (t = −0.46, N = 15, p=0.65).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: The number of workers involved in tool use did not have any effect on the total time of tool transport to the bait.
source: However, the number of workers involved in tool use did not have any effect on the latency to drop the first tool to the bait (t = 1.34, N = 15, p=0.20) nor on the total time of tool transport to the bait (t = −0.46, N = 15, p=0.65).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: The transport to the nest started always well after (124.4 ± 15.3 min) the completion of the tool transport to the bait.
source: The transport to the nest started always well after (124.4 ± 15.3 min, mean ± SE; Table 1) the completion of the tool transport to the bait.
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 1 presented in Table 1.

claim: Compared to the number of workers present in the foraging arena (23.33 ± 6.04 workers), only a few workers performed the tool use behaviour (2.33 ± 0.35 workers).
source: Compared to the number of workers present in the foraging arena (23.33 ± 6.04 workers, mean ± SE), only a few workers performed the tool use behaviour (2.33 ± 0.35 workers, mean ± SE; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 1 presented in Table 1.

claim: Workers repeatedly transported tools within the same trial and between trials.
source: We observed workers repeatedly transporting tools within the same trial and between trials (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by observational data from Experiment 1 presented in Table 2.

claim: Some workers participated in both parts of the task (transport of tools to the bait and also from the bait to the nests).
source: Some workers participated in both parts of the task (transport of tools to the bait and also from the bait to the nests) and repeated transports by the same worker were observed in both parts of the tool use process (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by observational data from Experiment 1 presented in Table 2.

claim: Repeated transports by the same worker were observed in both parts of the tool use process.
source: Some workers participated in both parts of the task (transport of tools to the bait and also from the bait to the nests) and repeated transports by the same worker were observed in both parts of the tool use process (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by observational data from Experiment 1 presented in Table 2.

claim: The tool users were not simply those workers that were the first to discover the location of the food and the tools.
source: In the next step, we asked whether the tool users were simply those workers that were the first to discover the location of the food and the tools. This was not the case.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that multiple workers contacted tools and food before the first tool user.

claim: An average of 11.35 ± 6.49 workers contacted the tools and the food before the first tool user dropped the first tool into the bait.
source: Indeed, an average of 11.35 ± 6.49 workers (mean ± SE, min = 3, max = 33 workers; see Table 3 for further details) contacted the tools and the food before the first tool user dropped the first tool into the bait.
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 1 presented in Table 3.

claim: Paint marked tool users took on average 388 ± 134.16 sec to locate the tools after contacting the food for the first time.
source: Paint marked tool users (N = 18) took on average 388 ± 134.16 sec (mean ± SE) to locate the tools after contacting the food for the first time.
evidence: This is supported by observational data from Experiment 1.

claim: Once tool users had the information about the location of both the food and tools, the latency to drop the first tool into the bait was 385.67 ± 128.30 sec.
source: Once they had the information about the location of both the food and tools, the latency to drop the first tool into the bait was 385.67 ± 128.30 sec (mean ± SE).
evidence: This is supported by observational data from Experiment 1.

claim: The latency to locate the tools after contacting the food and the latency to drop the first tool into the bait were not correlated.
source: However, these two latencies were not correlated (rs = −0.006, N = 18, p=0.98), meaning that those workers that located the tools earlier did not necessarily start the transport of tools to the bait faster.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data from Experiment 1.

claim: Workers that located the tools earlier did not necessarily start the transport of tools to the bait faster.
source: However, these two latencies were not correlated (rs = −0.006, N = 18, p=0.98), meaning that those workers that located the tools earlier did not necessarily start the transport of tools to the bait faster.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analysis from Experiment 1.

claim: About 20% of individually marked workers per sub-colony performed tool use during at least one of the four trials with 10 tools.
source: Of the 40 individually marked workers per sub-colony involved in this experiment, about 20% performed tool use during at least one of the four trials with 10 tools (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 2 presented in Table 4.

claim: The average number of individuals per sub-colony showing tool use was 8.25.
source: The average number of individuals per sub-colony showing tool use was 8.25 (CI95% [6.47, 10.03]).
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 2.

claim: The individual distribution of tool use events was not random in Experiment 2.
source: This was notably lower than 10.2 (CI95% [10.18, 10.22]), which is the average number of tool users obtained by randomly assigning the same number of observed tool use events to a simulated ant population based on the same number of individuals, sub-colonies and trials (see Simulation data of experiment 2, Supplementary file 1), and the confidence intervals do not overlap. This indicates that the individual distribution of tool use events was not random in our experiments.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of observed data with simulated random data.

claim: Of the 99 tool users in total, 64.7% performed several tool transports within the same trial.
source: Of the 99 tool users in total, 64.7% performed several tool transports within the same trial and 33.3% participated repetitively in more than one trial (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 2 presented in Table 4.

claim: Of the 99 tool users in total, 33.3% participated repetitively in more than one trial.
source: Of the 99 tool users in total, 64.7% performed several tool transports within the same trial and 33.3% participated repetitively in more than one trial (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 2 presented in Table 4.

claim: The occurrences of tool use were repeatable across trials at the individual level (RICC = 0.22, N = 1880, p=0.001).
source: It is important to note that the occurrences of tool use were repeatable across trials at the individual level (RICC = 0.22, N = 1880, p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of repeatability from Experiment 2.

claim: Half of the workers (50.38%) that performed tool use in the final trial with 20 tools also participated in at least one of the previous trials with 10 tools.
source: Half of the workers (50.38%) that performed tool use in the final trial with 20 tools, also participated in at least one of the previous trials with 10 tools (Table 6), thus confirming that the same ants use tools over and over again, including across trials.
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 2 presented in Table 6.

claim: The same ants use tools over and over again, including across trials.
source: Half of the workers (50.38%) that performed tool use in the final trial with 20 tools, also participated in at least one of the previous trials with 10 tools (Table 6), thus confirming that the same ants use tools over and over again, including across trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data from Experiment 2.

claim: Workers that performed tool use were not necessarily specialised in foraging for liquid food; they also transported cricket legs to the nest.
source: Workers that performed tool use were not necessarily specialised in foraging for liquid food; they also transported cricket legs to the nest.
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 2 showing overlap between tool users and cricket leg transporters.

claim: About half (48.31%) of the workers that transported cricket legs were also tool users in at least one trial.
source: About half (48.31%) of the workers that transported cricket legs were also tool users in at least one trial (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 2 presented in Table 4.

claim: Among the 99 tool users, 15 workers (15.15%) showed a particularly high activity by participating in at least two tool use trials and at least one cricket leg transport.
source: Among the 99 tool users, 15 workers (15.15%) showed a particularly high activity by participating in at least two tool use trials and at least one cricket leg transport (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 2 presented in Table 4.

claim: When workers consecutively transported four tools, the time to transport one tool decreased with the number of tools transported.
source: When workers consecutively transported four tools, the time to transport one tool decreased with the number of tools transported (second-third tool: LMM t = −2.25, N = 54, p=0.03, second-fourth tool: t = −3.75, p<0.001; Figure 1B, Source code 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data from Experiment 2 and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The average time to transport one tool did not change significantly between different trials.
source: However, the average time to transport one tool did not change significantly between different trials (first-second: t = −0.01, N = 29, p=0.99; first-third t = −1.02, p=0.32; Figure 1C, Source code 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data from Experiment 2 and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The interference of a new tool user did not alter the efficiency of the previous tool user.
source: The interference of this new tool user did not alter the efficiency of the previous tool user (LMM t = 0.5, N = 66, p=0.62), meaning that the time to transport a tool to the bait by the first worker did not change before and after interference, and there was no significant effect of the sub-colony (t = −0.52, N = 66, p=0.6).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data from Experiment 2.

claim: The time to transport a tool to the bait by the first worker did not change before and after interference by another worker.
source: The interference of this new tool user did not alter the efficiency of the previous tool user (LMM t = 0.5, N = 66, p=0.62), meaning that the time to transport a tool to the bait by the first worker did not change before and after interference, and there was no significant effect of the sub-colony (t = −0.52, N = 66, p=0.6).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical analysis from Experiment 2.

claim: The latency to bring the first tool to the bait was not different between the two types of sub-colonies (with and without pre-trial observation).
source: The latency to bring the first tool to the bait was not different between the two types of sub-colonies (LMM t = −0.5, N = 12, p=0.64; Figure 2A, Source code 1) as well as the total time of tool transport (t = −0.88, N = 12, p=0.42; Figure 2B, Source code 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data from Experiment 2 and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The total time of tool transport was not different between the two types of sub-colonies (with and without pre-trial observation).
source: The latency to bring the first tool to the bait was not different between the two types of sub-colonies (LMM t = −0.5, N = 12, p=0.64; Figure 2A, Source code 1) as well as the total time of tool transport (t = −0.88, N = 12, p=0.42; Figure 2B, Source code 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data from Experiment 2 and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The number of workers involved in tool use was not different between the two groups of sub-colonies (with and without pre-trial observation).
source: The number of workers involved in tool use was also not different between the two groups (LMM t = −0.46, N = 12, p=0.67), indicating that there is no social learning in these conditions.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data from Experiment 2.

claim: There is no social learning in tool use under the experimental conditions of Experiment 2.
source: The number of workers involved in tool use was also not different between the two groups (LMM t = −0.46, N = 12, p=0.67), indicating that there is no social learning in these conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results from Experiment 2.

claim: Ants showed significant consistency over time in their behavioural responses in the open-field test.
source: Ants showed significant consistency over time in their behavioural responses. In the open-field test, the time spent walking in the periphery (RICC = 0.27, N = 154, CI95% [0.11, 0.41], p<0.001) and the total time spent in the central area were significantly repeatable across the two sessions (RICC = 0.43, N = 154, CI95% [0.31, 0.56], p<0.0001; Figure 3C, Source code 1).
evidence: This is supported by repeatability analysis of data from Experiment 3 and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the open-field test, the time spent walking in the periphery was significantly repeatable across the two sessions (RICC = 0.27, N = 154, CI95% [0.11, 0.41], p<0.001).
source: In the open-field test, the time spent walking in the periphery (RICC = 0.27, N = 154, CI95% [0.11, 0.41], p<0.001) and the total time spent in the central area were significantly repeatable across the two sessions (RICC = 0.43, N = 154, CI95% [0.31, 0.56], p<0.0001; Figure 3C, Source code 1).
evidence: This is supported by repeatability analysis of data from Experiment 3 and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the open-field test, the total time spent in the central area was significantly repeatable across the two sessions (RICC = 0.43, N = 154, CI95% [0.31, 0.56], p<0.0001).
source: In the open-field test, the time spent walking in the periphery (RICC = 0.27, N = 154, CI95% [0.11, 0.41], p<0.001) and the total time spent in the central area were significantly repeatable across the two sessions (RICC = 0.43, N = 154, CI95% [0.31, 0.56], p<0.0001; Figure 3C, Source code 1).
evidence: This is supported by repeatability analysis of data from Experiment 3 and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the reaction to prey test, the time spent in contact with the prey was highly repeatable (RICC = 0.61, N = 154, CI95% [0.49, 0.71], p<0.0001).
source: In the reaction to prey test, the time spent in contact with the prey was also highly repeatable (RICC = 0.61, N = 154, CI95% [0.49, 0.71], p<0.0001; Figure 3D, Source code 2).
evidence: This is supported by repeatability analysis of data from Experiment 3 and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The time spent in contact with the prey was negatively correlated with the time spent walking in the periphery (rs = −0.30, N = 154, p<0.001).
source: The time spent in contact with the prey was negatively correlated with the time spent walking in the periphery (rs = −0.30, N = 154, p<0.001) and positively correlated with the total time spent in the central area (rs = 0.33, N = 154, p<0.001), indicating that the more exploratory ants were also those more interested in the prey.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of data from Experiment 3.

claim: The time spent in contact with the prey was positively correlated with the total time spent in the central area (rs = 0.33, N = 154, p<0.001).
source: The time spent in contact with the prey was negatively correlated with the time spent walking in the periphery (rs = −0.30, N = 154, p<0.001) and positively correlated with the total time spent in the central area (rs = 0.33, N = 154, p<0.001), indicating that the more exploratory ants were also those more interested in the prey.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of data from Experiment 3.

claim: The more exploratory ants were also those more interested in the prey.
source: The time spent in contact with the prey was negatively correlated with the time spent walking in the periphery (rs = −0.30, N = 154, p<0.001) and positively correlated with the total time spent in the central area (rs = 0.33, N = 154, p<0.001), indicating that the more exploratory ants were also those more interested in the prey.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analysis from Experiment 3.

claim: The ants' personality score significantly predicted the probability of using tools in at least one trial (GLMM z = 3.97, N = 154, p<0.001).
source: The ants' personality score significantly predicted the probability of using tools in at least one trial (GLMM z = 3.97, N = 154, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data from Experiment 3.

claim: The confidence intervals of the personality score of tool users (mean = 0.57, CI95% [0.26, 0.88]) and non-tool users (mean = −0.33, CI95% [−0.56,–0.09]) did not overlap.
source: Moreover, the confidence intervals of the personality score of tool users (mean = 0.57, CI95% [0.26, 0.88]) and non-tool users (mean = −0.33, CI95% [−0.56,–0.09]) did not overlap (Figure 5C, Source code 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data from Experiment 3 and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A positive personality score characterised those ants that spent more time exploring the central area in the open field test and that spent more time in contact with the prey.
source: A positive personality score characterised those ants that spent more time exploring the central area in the open field test and that spent more time in contact with the prey (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The latency to bring the first tool to the bait was 894.71 ± 153.49 sec in Experiment 3.
source: The latency to bring the first tool to the bait was 894.71 ± 153.49 sec (mean ± SE, N = 21 trials; see 'Contact_with_tools' in data of experiment 3, Supplementary file 1), which gives plenty of time for all the ants to explore and find the tools.
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 3.

claim: In only five out of 21 occasions, the tool user was the first worker to investigate the tools.
source: From a total of 21 trials, only in five occasions, the tool user was the first worker to investigate the tools.
evidence: This is supported by observational data from Experiment 3.

claim: In the majority of the trials (16 out of 21) an average of about five workers investigated the tools by antennation before the first tool user but did not pick them up.
source: In the majority of the trials (16 out of 21) an average of about five workers investigated the tools by antennation before the first tool user but did not pick them up (4.94 ± 0.52 (mean ± SE) workers, min = 1 worker, max = 8 workers).
evidence: This is supported by observational data from Experiment 3.

claim: The tool use behaviour is not merely prompted by the fact of finding the tools or the food before other workers.
source: This indicates that the tool use behaviour is not merely prompted by the fact of finding the tools or the food before other workers.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that multiple workers investigated tools before the first tool user.

claim: There was a positive correlation between the latency to find the prey and the time spent in contact with the prey in the reaction to prey test.
source: In contrast, we found a positive correlation between the latency to find the prey and the time spent in contact with the prey: the longer the latency, the longer the time spent with the prey (session 1: rs = 0.27, N = 154, p<0.001; session 2: rs = 0.42, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of data from Experiment 3.

claim: Tool users typically transported more than one tool to the bait.
source: Tool users typically transported more than one tool to the bait.
evidence: This is supported by observational data from Experiment 3.

claim: In most of the cases, the transport of all the 10 tools was performed by one worker.
source: In most of the cases, the transport of all the 10 tools was performed by one worker, in 23% of the cases by two workers and only in one case by three workers.
evidence: This is supported by observational data from Experiment 3.

claim: The removal of the active workers after each trial did not influence the characteristics of the tool transport to the bait compared to the first trial.
source: The removal of the active workers after each trial did not influence the characteristics of the tool transport to the bait compared to the first trial (latency of first tool to bait: LMM −0.7 < t < 0.94, N = 28, p>0.36; total transport time: LMM −0.7 < t < 1.02, p>0.32; number of workers involved: GLMM−0.66 < z < −0.07, N = 28, p>0.51).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data from Experiment 3.

claim: The workers that took over the tool use task were not significantly less efficient than the removed tool users.
source: Therefore, the workers that took over the tool use task were not significantly less efficient than the removed tool users.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results from Experiment 3.

claim: In the final trial with 20 tools, a total of 18 workers used tools.
source: In the final trial with 20 tools, a total of 18 workers used tools.
evidence: This is supported by observational data from Experiment 3.

claim: Of the 18 workers that used tools in the final trial, 12 workers (66.6%) previously performed tool transport.
source: Of these, 12 workers (66.6%) previously performed tool transport and they brought 106 (66.25%) of the 160 tools that were transported to the bait in this last trial.
evidence: This is supported by observational data from Experiment 3.

claim: The 12 workers that previously performed tool transport brought 106 (66.25%) of the 160 tools that were transported to the bait in the final trial.
source: Of these, 12 workers (66.6%) previously performed tool transport and they brought 106 (66.25%) of the 160 tools that were transported to the bait in this last trial.
evidence: This is supported by observational data from Experiment 3.

claim: Of the 34 workers removed during the first 3 days of the experiment, 11 resumed tool using in the final trial.
source: Of the 34 workers removed during the first 3 days of the experiment, 11 resumed tool using in this last trial, and 4 of these workers were active during the first trial with 10 tools 7 days earlier.
evidence: This is supported by observational data from Experiment 3.

claim: Four of the workers that resumed tool use in the final trial were active during the first trial with 10 tools 7 days earlier.
source: Of the 34 workers removed during the first 3 days of the experiment, 11 resumed tool using in this last trial, and 4 of these workers were active during the first trial with 10 tools 7 days earlier.
evidence: This is supported by observational data from Experiment 3.

claim: Tool use is not a stochastic phenomenon but it is performed by a subset of workers with specific behavioural traits.
source: In sum, our data indicate that tool use is not a stochastic phenomenon but it is performed by a subset of workers with specific behavioural traits.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined results of all three experiments.

claim: Covering the food quickly with debris gives an advantage to Aphaenogaster ants in the competition with more dominant ant species.
source: In natural conditions, covering the food quickly with debris gives an advantage to Aphaenogaster ants in the competition with more dominant ant species, which cannot exploit the food once it is covered (Fellers and Fellers, 1976), thus leaving plenty of time for Aphaenogaster to bring the food-imbibed tools to the nest.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fellers and Fellers, 1976.

claim: More dominant ant species cannot exploit the food once it is covered with debris.
source: In natural conditions, covering the food quickly with debris gives an advantage to Aphaenogaster ants in the competition with more dominant ant species, which cannot exploit the food once it is covered (Fellers and Fellers, 1976), thus leaving plenty of time for Aphaenogaster to bring the food-imbibed tools to the nest.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fellers and Fellers, 1976.

claim: It appears to be advantageous to first completely cover the food with debris and then to start transporting them to the nest.
source: Therefore, it appears to be advantageous to first completely cover the food with debris and then to start transporting them to the nest.
evidence: This is an inference based on the competitive advantage and the observed temporal pattern of tool use.

claim: Task specialisation does not translate into higher performance in ant species without morphologically differentiated workers.
source: This may not hinder efficiency since it has been shown that task specialisation does not translate into higher performance in ant species without morphologically differentiated workers (Dornhaus, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dornhaus, 2008.

claim: Spontaneous tool use and manufacture has been shown in naive juvenile New Caledonian crows.
source: Spontaneous tool use and manufacture has been also shown in vertebrates, such as naive juvenile New Caledonian crows (Kenward et al., 2005), while social learning appears to be essential when the task is complex and non-natural, as observed in bumblebees (Alem et al., 2016; Loukola et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kenward et al., 2005.

claim: Social learning appears to be essential when the task is complex and non-natural, as observed in bumblebees.
source: Spontaneous tool use and manufacture has been also shown in vertebrates, such as naive juvenile New Caledonian crows (Kenward et al., 2005), while social learning appears to be essential when the task is complex and non-natural, as observed in bumblebees (Alem et al., 2016; Loukola et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alem et al., 2016 and Loukola et al., 2017.

claim: Aphaenogaster ants are able to select among different types of tools according to their soaking capacity and the environmental context.
source: We know that Aphaenogaster ants are able to select among different types of tools according to their soaking capacity and the environmental context (Maák et al., 2017; Lőrinczi et al., 2018) and that they learn to choose the optimal tools over successive trials (Maák et al., 2017), therefore we cannot exclude that social learning could play a role in the process of tool selection, a possibility that awaits formal testing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maák et al., 2017 and Lőrinczi et al., 2018.

claim: Aphaenogaster ants learn to choose the optimal tools over successive trials.
source: We know that Aphaenogaster ants are able to select among different types of tools according to their soaking capacity and the environmental context (Maák et al., 2017; Lőrinczi et al., 2018) and that they learn to choose the optimal tools over successive trials (Maák et al., 2017), therefore we cannot exclude that social learning could play a role in the process of tool selection, a possibility that awaits formal testing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maák et al., 2017.

claim: Social learning could play a role in the process of tool selection in Aphaenogaster ants.
source: We know that Aphaenogaster ants are able to select among different types of tools according to their soaking capacity and the environmental context (Maák et al., 2017; Lőrinczi et al., 2018) and that they learn to choose the optimal tools over successive trials (Maák et al., 2017), therefore we cannot exclude that social learning could play a role in the process of tool selection, a possibility that awaits formal testing.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possibility that has not been tested.

claim: Consistent inter-individual behavioural variation has been shown in other ant species.
source: Consistent inter-individual behavioural variation has also been shown in other ant species (e.g. Kühbandner et al., 2014; Udino et al., 2017) and it might be a general characteristic of workers.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kühbandner et al., 2014 and Udino et al., 2017.

claim: Consistent inter-individual behavioural variation might be a general characteristic of ant workers.
source: Consistent inter-individual behavioural variation has also been shown in other ant species (e.g. Kühbandner et al., 2014; Udino et al., 2017) and it might be a general characteristic of workers.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on observations in multiple species.

claim: Individual behavioural variability is directly linked to the probability to perform a certain task in A. senilis.
source: What is new in our work is the discovery that individual behavioural variability is directly linked to the probability to perform a certain task, in this case tool use.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the results of Experiment 3.

claim: Workers with a positive personality score were more likely to be involved in tool use than workers with a less positive or negative personality score.
source: Workers with a positive personality score, characterised by high explorative behaviour and prey-attraction, were more likely to be involved in tool use than workers with a less positive or negative personality score.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of personality and tool use data from Experiment 3.

claim: According to the 'response threshold model', workers characterised by a low threshold will respond to low stimulus intensity (high responsiveness), while workers with high threshold will respond to high stimulus intensity (low responsiveness).
source: According to the 'response threshold model' (Robinson, 1992; Beshers and Fewell, 2001), workers characterised by a low threshold will respond to low stimulus intensity (high responsiveness), while workers with high threshold will respond to high stimulus intensity (low responsiveness) (Bonabeau et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical model supported by citations.

claim: Experience may act as 'self-reinforcement' and directly modulate the individual response threshold.
source: Experience may act as 'self-reinforcement' and directly modulate the individual response threshold.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about mechanisms underlying behavioral variability.

claim: The simple fact of performing a task would lower the corresponding stimulus threshold, while not performing a task would further increase the individual threshold.
source: It was hypothesised that the simple fact of performing a task would lower the corresponding stimulus threshold, while not performing a task would further increase the individual threshold (Theraulaz et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Theraulaz et al., 1998.

claim: In clonal ants, foragers that were successful had a higher probability to perform the foraging task again, compared to unsuccessful foragers, which specialised in brood care.
source: Indeed, a study using clonal ants showed that, all else being equal, foragers that were successful had a higher probability to perform the foraging task again, compared to unsuccessful foragers, which specialised in brood care (Ravary et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ravary et al., 2007.

claim: Individual personality differences within a given behavioural group may contribute to a fine-tuned division of labour.
source: Individual personality differences within a given behavioural group (foragers, nurses) may contribute to a fine-tuned division of labour but this possibility is relatively unexplored.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the potential role of personality in division of labour.

claim: A study in honeybees found evidence for life-long personality differences in workers.
source: A study in honeybees found evidence for life-long personality differences in workers and suggested that the response thresholds to some stimuli could be related to personality type, thus contributing to more robust inter-individual behavioural differences leading to division of labour even when individuals age together or share similar experiences (Walton and Toth, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walton and Toth, 2016.

claim: Response thresholds to some stimuli could be related to personality type in honeybees.
source: A study in honeybees found evidence for life-long personality differences in workers and suggested that the response thresholds to some stimuli could be related to personality type, thus contributing to more robust inter-individual behavioural differences leading to division of labour even when individuals age together or share similar experiences (Walton and Toth, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walton and Toth, 2016.

claim: In carpenter ants, there is evidence for inter-individual variability in sucrose responsiveness and learning success in different behavioural groups of workers performing different tasks.
source: In carpenter ants, there is evidence for inter-individual variability in sucrose responsiveness and learning success in different behavioural groups of workers performing different tasks (Perez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Perez et al., 2013.

claim: In the ant Myrmica rubra, individual personality differences are connected to spatial fidelity (the position in the nest).
source: In the ant Myrmica rubra, individual personality differences are connected to spatial fidelity (the position in the nest) and ants located in a given position show low thresholds to perform tasks associated with that position, thus generating division of labour (Pamminger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pamminger et al., 2014.

claim: In Myrmica rubra, ants located in a given position show low thresholds to perform tasks associated with that position, thus generating division of labour.
source: In the ant Myrmica rubra, individual personality differences are connected to spatial fidelity (the position in the nest) and ants located in a given position show low thresholds to perform tasks associated with that position, thus generating division of labour (Pamminger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pamminger et al., 2014.

claim: A. senilis colonies could cope well with the removal of active tool users, which were immediately replaced by individuals that were previously less active.
source: We found that A. senilis colonies could cope well with the removal of active tool users, which were immediately replaced by individuals that were previously less active.
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 3 showing that new workers took over tool use after removal of active workers.

claim: In the red harvester ant, Pogonomyrmex barbatus, when the most active foragers were experimentally removed they were replaced by other individuals.
source: Similarly, in the red harvester ant, Pogonomyrmex barbatus, when the most active foragers were experimentally removed they were replaced by other individuals (Beverly et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beverly et al., 2009.

claim: In the ant Temnothorax rugatulus, when the most active nurses and foragers were removed they were quickly replaced by workers from the reserve pool of inactive individuals.
source: In the ant Temnothorax rugatulus as well, when the most active nurses and foragers were removed they were quickly replaced by workers from the reserve pool of inactive individuals (Charbonneau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Charbonneau et al., 2017.

claim: In T. albipennis, 20% of ants were more active and performed transports repeatedly in successive experimental emigration trials.
source: In T. albipennis, in the context of nest emigration, 20% of ants were more active and performed transports repeatedly in successive experimental emigration trials (Pinter-Wollman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pinter-Wollman et al., 2012.

claim: In T. albipennis, removed active ants were replaced by previously less active individuals, but when they were returned to the colony they did not resume their active role.
source: Removed active ants were replaced by previously less active individuals, but when they were returned to the colony they did not resume their active role, they were thus permanently replaced.
evidence: This is supported by citation context referring to Pinter-Wollman et al., 2012.

claim: Modifications in the social context and experience can cause a long-lasting change in the response threshold of workers.
source: The authors suggest that modifications in the social context and experience can cause a long-lasting change in the response threshold of workers (Pinter-Wollman et al., 2012; Jeanson, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pinter-Wollman et al., 2012 and Jeanson, 2019.

claim: In A. senilis, many of the removed active workers resumed tool use when they were returned to their sub-colony in the last trial with 20 tools.
source: This is not what we observed in A. senilis, in which many of the removed active workers resumed tool use when they were returned to their sub-colony in the last trial with 20 tools, including workers that were removed 10 days earlier (after the very first trial).
evidence: This is supported by observational data from Experiment 3.

claim: The probability to perform tool use in A. senilis is linked to personality, which, by definition, is consistent over time.
source: This is not surprising if we consider that the probability to perform tool use in A. senilis is linked to personality, which, by definition, is consistent over time.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the definition of personality and the experimental findings.

claim: The involvement of workers with appropriate personality ensures high efficiency in tool use.
source: In conclusion, our work shows that instead of extreme task specialisation, the involvement of workers with appropriate personality ensures high efficiency in tool use.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined results of the experiments.

claim: Colony-level personality exists in A. senilis.
source: Previous studies demonstrated the existence of colony-level personality in A. senilis (Blight et al., 2016a; Blight et al., 2016b), we thus predicted that consistent behavioural differences will be found also at the individual level in this species (worker personality).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blight et al., 2016a and Blight et al., 2016b.

claim: Aphaenogaster senilis is a monogynous Mediterranean ant species.
source: Twelve colonies of the monogynous Mediterranean ant species, Aphaenogaster senilis, were used.
evidence: This is a factual description of the study species.

claim: Aphaenogaster senilis occurs in open and sunny locations (e.g. forest edges, lawns, fields, sand dune areas).
source: This species occurs in open and sunny locations (e.g. forest edges, lawns, fields, sand dune areas), and colony size varies between a few hundred to a few thousand workers (Boulay et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boulay et al., 2007.

claim: Colony size of Aphaenogaster senilis varies between a few hundred to a few thousand workers.
source: This species occurs in open and sunny locations (e.g. forest edges, lawns, fields, sand dune areas), and colony size varies between a few hundred to a few thousand workers (Boulay et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boulay et al., 2007.

claim: Ants were collected in the Doñana National Park (Spain) in March 2019.
source: Ants were collected in the Doñana National Park (Spain) in March 2019 and kept at the Laboratory of Experimental and Comparative Ethology (University Sorbonne Paris Nord, France) under standard conditions (temperature 24 ± 4°C; relative humidity 50–60%; natural light cycle).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the methods.

claim: In A. rudis, no evidence of task partitioning was found.
source: In A. rudis, similarly to A. senilis, no evidence of task partitioning was found (Banschbach et al., 2006), although task partitioning was suggested in earlier observations of A. famelica (Tanaka and Ono, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Banschbach et al., 2006.

claim: Task partitioning was suggested in earlier observations of A. famelica.
source: In A. rudis, similarly to A. senilis, no evidence of task partitioning was found (Banschbach et al., 2006), although task partitioning was suggested in earlier observations of A. famelica (Tanaka and Ono, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tanaka and Ono, 1978.

claim: Naïve foragers can carry out tool use in A. famelica.
source: Our finding is in agreement with the observation by Tanaka and Ono, 1978 that naïve foragers can carry out tool use in A. famelica.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tanaka and Ono, 1978.
